purpose: Extend the reviewed live roadmap with the durable SalvageNet product direction while preserving H02A as the sole active task.

milestones.title: M1.5 — Turnkey cluster MVP
milestones.description: One signed configuration turns a validated phone substrate into a native worker for an existing orchestrator, with a thin Slint controller and an unattended safety floor.

milestones.title: M5 — Community-owned infrastructure
milestones.description: Account-linked invitations, user-owned data placement, and optional community-operated discovery services.

items.title: Define the signed provisioning capsule and native attachment contract
items.summary: Make one authenticated, immutable configuration the user-facing entry point while preserving each runtime, overlay, and orchestrator's native configuration format.
items.outcome: A controller can compose, sign, transfer, validate, cache, and idempotently apply one capsule that selects a runtime/profile, references native overlay configuration, references a native orchestrator attachment, and names a host policy.
items.whyNow: The product promise is turnkey device attachment, not merely remote VM control. Establishing the narrow envelope prevents later UIs and tools from inventing incompatible configuration models.
nonGoals: No universal workload schema, scheduler, service model, or replacement for Kubernetes, Nomad, Docker, Nix, OpenTofu, Ansible, or native configuration files.
validation: Signature, expiry, rollback, secret-reference, offline-cache, idempotency, and native-config round-trip tests pass.

items.title: Prove one-config Docker Swarm attachment on stock Android
items.summary: Use the stock APK and QEMU backend to turn one phone into a real Docker Engine Swarm worker from one signed capsule.
items.outcome: A physical phone imports one capsule, boots its qualified Linux environment, joins Docker Engine Swarm mode as a worker, runs a replicated service, remains useful while the configuration laptop is offline, and drains, leaves, and rejoins cleanly.
items.whyNow: A validated node substrate is necessary but not sufficient evidence of SalvageNet's user value. Swarm mode has a small native join surface and is the fastest honest proof that upstream orchestration remains authoritative.
nonGoals: No raw SwarmKit embedding, custom scheduler, Compose abstraction, or Swarm service objects in the Host API.
validation: Join, certificate issuance, service placement, controller-offline continuity, drain, leave, replacement, and rejoin pass on one exact phone/APK/capsule evidence set.

items.title: Ship a thin Slint provisioning controller
items.summary: Provide a polished cross-platform Slint flow for composing/importing capsules, enrolling nodes, observing progress, opening native tools, and exporting safe diagnostics.
items.outcome: A desktop controller guides one-config setup and the Swarm proof without owning cluster desired state or changing the existing Host API merely to justify a UI rewrite.
items.whyNow: The controller is the primary user experience, while the current Python CLI is intentionally temporary. A thin UI can make the real workflow demonstrable without delaying Android physical validation or rewriting the Android lifecycle shell.
nonGoals: No cluster dashboard clone, Android host rewrite, browser-held keys, or proprietary workload-management model.
validation: Capsule, enrollment, lifecycle, recovery, accessibility, packaging, and offline-controller UX tests pass.

items.title: Compose provisioning with Nix and OpenTofu modules
items.summary: Let advanced users declaratively compose native cluster, network, artifact, and host inputs without requiring Nix or OpenTofu on the phone.
items.outcome: Pinned Nix modules and OpenTofu modules produce the same signed capsule and native artifacts as the UI, reuse existing providers where available, and avoid remote-exec provisioning as the normal path.
items.whyNow: Turnkey should reduce scripts and duplicate files without flattening native tools. A build-time composition layer gives reproducibility and an expert escape hatch while keeping the node runtime small.
nonGoals: No first-party OpenTofu provider until real remotely managed resource state justifies one; no Nix runtime requirement in the APK.
validation: Reference Swarm, K3s-ready, overlay, artifact, and host-policy compositions produce deterministic capsule digests and native files.

items.title: Qualify the minimum unattended safety and continuity floor
items.summary: Before early access, prove the stock-phone node remains understandable and safe through screen-off, Doze, power, thermal, storage, process, network, and controller disruptions.
items.outcome: The primary device completes a bounded soak with explicit wake policy, external-power transitions, thermal throttling and emergency stop, storage reserve, process recovery, and configuration-authority absence.
items.whyNow: A successful boot and join do not establish that an old phone is suitable for unattended self-hosting. This is the minimum safety floor; the broader OEM and performance matrix remains later reliability work.
nonGoals: No universal OEM support, indefinite battery operation, opaque device score, or claim that stock Android can be made unkillable.
validation: Screen-off/Doze, wake, charging loss/recovery, thermal stop, low-storage, process death, network loss, offline authority, and soak evidence pass on the exact candidate.

items.title: Generalize the host contract to execution environments
items.summary: Evolve additive public vocabulary from VM-only resources to a capability-aware execution-environment contract while preserving the proven QEMU path.
items.outcome: QEMU, native system-container, Linux service/container/VM, and WSL adapters can satisfy common lifecycle, observation, data-ownership, diagnostics, and attachment contracts without pretending every backend is a VM.
items.whyNow: QEMU is the correct first backend but not the whole product. The contract should broaden only after the stock proof establishes real semantics and before later platforms duplicate VM-shaped APIs.
nonGoals: No speculative universal runtime, removal of QEMU evidence, raw backend arguments, or compatibility layer for unpublished alpha APIs without an explicit need.
validation: An additive contract and conformance suite preserve QEMU behavior and are implementable by at least one structurally different backend.

items.title: Add the my-avbroot-setup patched-Android system backend
items.summary: Use the existing AVB patch workflow to install a narrowly scoped init daemon and efficient native Linux/container backend without making patched Android mandatory.
items.outcome: The same APK and capsule bind to an AVB-installed daemon with a dedicated SELinux domain, structured Binder or equivalent API, boot persistence, update/rollback integration, and no general-purpose root shell.
items.whyNow: Patched Android is priority B after the stock APK path and can materially improve efficiency and unattended reliability. It is a first-class backend, not merely a policy tier.
nonGoals: No requirement to patch stock devices, arbitrary su service, hidden downgrade of stock support, or unbounded privileged command interface.
validation: Patch, install, SELinux, API authentication, runtime lifecycle, boot, update, rollback, revocation, and recovery pass on a supported device.

items.title: Add verified-boot and device attestation trust tiers
items.summary: Bind hardware-backed device identity, Android RootOfTrust evidence, recognized custom AVB keys, APK identity, and signed build manifests into explicit trust tiers.
items.outcome: The controller distinguishes vendor-verified, custom-key locked, unlocked measured, software-measured, and unattested nodes without claiming an unlocked bootloader is equivalent to a locked verified chain.
items.whyNow: Community and multi-owner clusters need understandable admission facts, especially when custom ROM patching is supported. Trust evidence should inform policy without excluding useful lower-trust devices by default.
nonGoals: No binary trusted/untrusted claim, Play Integrity dependency, permanent hardware identifier collection, or false equivalence between unlocked and locked boot states.
validation: Challenge freshness, application identity, verifiedBootKey/state/hash, lock state, build-manifest matching, downgrade, privacy, and policy tests pass.

items.title: Create the native SBC host and stable-cell role
items.summary: Run the shared host agent natively on ARM64 SBCs so they can be workers, stable orchestrator managers, routers, caches, ingress nodes, and USB peers.
items.outcome: A simple service installation applies the same capsule and attachment contracts with native Linux execution and publishes stable-node capabilities separately from phone reliability classes.
items.whyNow: SBCs are priority C and provide the stable quorum, ingress, artifact, and physical-link roles that highly available phone clusters should not force onto stock Android workers.
nonGoals: No assumption that every SBC is control-plane suitable and no custom orchestrator manager implementation.
validation: Install, upgrade, capsule apply, native runtime, orchestrator role, offline authority, diagnostics, and removal tests pass on one representative ARM64 SBC.

items.title: Support existing Linux hosts through native, container, VM, and microsandbox modes
items.summary: Bring older computers into SalvageNet with the lightest suitable supported execution mode while preserving the same authority, attachment, diagnostics, and data-ownership boundaries.
items.outcome: A Linux service can select native process, OCI container, VM, or bounded microsandbox adapters from measured capabilities and install through ordinary packages or a containerized path.
items.whyNow: Existing Linux machines are priority D and expand useful capacity without Android constraints. They also provide the second concrete platform needed to keep shared contracts honest.
nonGoals: No requirement that all modes expose identical low-level capabilities and no replacement for systemd, OpenRC, Podman, containerd, QEMU, or native service managers.
validation: Host conformance, installation, least-privilege mode selection, lifecycle, upgrade, rollback, data continuity, and orchestrator attachment pass on old and current Linux hosts.

items.title: Build a custom Linux appliance image
items.summary: Produce a minimal declarative Linux image for dedicated SalvageNet nodes after native Linux requirements and artifact trust are evidenced.
items.outcome: A reproducible image boots into the shared host agent, applies signed capsules, supports atomic update/rollback, and remains compatible with native orchestrator agents and standard debugging tools.
items.whyNow: A custom OS is priority E, but building it before the Android and existing-Linux contracts settle would freeze guesses into a distribution. It follows concrete platform evidence.
nonGoals: No new general-purpose Linux distribution, private package ecosystem, or custom init/container/network stack without a demonstrated gap.
validation: Reproducible build, secure boot where available, install, capsule apply, update, rollback, recovery, and orchestrator conformance pass.

items.title: Support Windows through WSL
items.summary: Install the Linux host agent and supported runtime modes inside WSL while a small native bridge handles setup, startup, networking, and recovery where Windows integration is required.
items.outcome: A Windows user can attach a WSL node through the same capsule and native orchestrator configuration without a separate Windows workload-management model.
items.whyNow: WSL is priority F and should reuse the Linux platform rather than create a first-party Windows runtime before higher-priority hosts work.
nonGoals: No native Windows container orchestrator, Hyper-V replacement, or duplicate non-Linux node agent.
validation: Install, startup, localhost/LAN networking, shutdown, update, data persistence, and external orchestrator attachment pass on supported WSL versions.

items.title: Add a native Nomad client attachment
items.summary: Prove Nomad client join, allocation continuity, drain, leave, disconnected behavior, and recovery through official Nomad configuration and task drivers.
items.outcome: A qualified full Linux environment becomes a replaceable Nomad client without Nomad jobs, scheduling, service discovery, or server state entering the Host API.
items.whyNow: Nomad is a distinct orchestrator family and validates that the attachment boundary is not merely Docker- or Kubernetes-shaped. It follows the simpler Swarm proof.
nonGoals: No Nomad server inside the APK, jobspec abstraction, unsupported user-namespace client mode, or hidden licensing assumption.
validation: Native HCL, capability checks, join, allocation, controller/server interruption, drain, leave, rejoin, and recovery evidence pass.

items.title: Evaluate Zenoh as an optional bootstrap and discovery fabric
items.summary: Test Zenoh peer, client, and router modes for intermittent controllers, node presence, bounded status queries, peer-assisted capsule retrieval, and cell gateways.
items.outcome: A reviewed spike determines whether Zenoh should supplement HTTPS and the overlay for bootstrap/discovery while signed capsules and upstream orchestrators remain authoritative.
items.whyNow: Zenoh matches future offline and cell topologies, but adding a distributed fabric before the physical and Swarm proofs would increase failure modes without proving product value.
nonGoals: No replacement for Tailscale/Headscale, CRDT desired state, cluster scheduler, application data plane, or mandatory broker/router.
validation: Android and Linux integration size, lifecycle, peer/router recovery, access control, tailnet and USB traversal, query/liveliness semantics, and offline-capsule tests produce an adopt/hold/reject ADR.

items.title: Bootstrap Headscale on the first eligible node through dynamic DNS
items.summary: Offer an optional path where a reachable first node runs Headscale, registers a dynamic DNS name, obtains trusted TLS, and publishes enough signed discovery data for the controller to connect.
items.outcome: A controller with no existing Headscale service can provision a public-reachable phone guest, SBC, or Linux node as the initial coordination server and then enroll later nodes without making that topology mandatory.
items.whyNow: This reduces setup friction for self-hosters, but it is lower priority than proving attachment to an existing coordination service and must state that DNS does not solve NAT or CGNAT reachability.
nonGoals: No claim that DDNS traverses CGNAT, no mandatory public exposure, no automatic manager promotion, and no dependence on a SalvageNet-operated DNS service.
validation: Reachability detection, DNS update, ACME/TLS, Headscale health, first enrollment, controller rediscovery, address change, backup/restore, loss, and safe fallback tests pass on eligible and ineligible networks.

items.title: Add signed QR invitations and account-linked device enrollment
items.summary: Let communities issue scoped, expiring invitations so a person can bind an authenticated account and hardware-backed device key to a node and permitted roles.
items.outcome: Distinct QR invitations support one-time redemption, account login, device-key binding, attestation evidence, community membership, revocation, and privacy-preserving role assignment.
items.whyNow: Community clusters need a usable ownership and consent model before personal devices or storage can be safely scheduled. This follows production principal and attestation foundations.
nonGoals: No permanent cluster credential in a QR code, hidden device fingerprinting, mandatory centralized SalvageNet account service, or unrestricted invitation role.
validation: Invitation signing, expiry, replay, PKCE/OIDC flow, device-key binding, attestation policy, revocation, recovery, consent, and privacy tests pass.

items.title: Define user-owned storage locality and availability policies
items.summary: Map a person's app data to their own devices where applications and upstream orchestrators can support it, with explicit local-only, encrypted-backup, and replicated-HA choices.
items.outcome: The controller generates native placement, volume, backup, and application guidance that makes physical locality versus availability trade-offs visible and recoverable.
items.whyNow: Personal device ownership is a core future community use case, but it must build on real accounts, node identity, storage evidence, and upstream volume mechanisms rather than a custom distributed filesystem.
nonGoals: No promise that data can remain exclusively on an offline phone and remain highly available, no row-level sharding of arbitrary applications, and no new distributed storage engine by default.
validation: At least one native orchestrator path proves local-only, encrypted-backup, and replicated policies with loss, reconnect, restore, consent, and clear availability behavior.

items.title: Offer an optional community dynamic-DNS service
items.summary: Provide a narrowly scoped open service for communities that need stable names for eligible self-hosted coordination or ingress nodes without tying SalvageNet to one commercial DDNS provider.
items.outcome: Communities can delegate names, update authenticated records, rotate credentials, apply abuse controls, export zones, and migrate to another provider while node software remains provider-neutral.
items.whyNow: A community service may reduce onboarding friction after the self-hosted first-node flow is proven. It should not become a prerequisite or conceal reachability requirements.
nonGoals: No NAT traversal promise, general-purpose DNS hosting business, forced telemetry, or hard dependency on a SalvageNet-operated service.
validation: Authenticated update, delegation, rate limit, abuse, privacy, DNSSEC/zone-export feasibility, provider migration, outage, and deletion tests pass before public operation.
